lesson.title: MAC Addresses: The Identity Built Into Every Interface
lesson.summary: Explains the MAC address as the fixed, hardware level identifier assigned to a network interface, used for local delivery on a physical network segment.
lesson.body:
Every network interface, the attachment point introduced in the previous section, is given a unique identifier so that other devices on the same local network can address it directly. That identifier is called a MAC address, short for Media Access Control address. A MAC address is typically 48 bits long and is conventionally written as six pairs of hexadecimal digits separated by colons, for example 3C:A6:2F:5B:9D:14. Unlike the IP address covered next, a MAC address is generally assigned by the interface's manufacturer at the time it is built, burned into the hardware, which is why you will sometimes hear it called a physical address or a hardware address.

A MAC address is structured in two parts. The first half identifies the manufacturer, through a code called an organizationally unique identifier assigned by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, and the second half is a unique value that manufacturer assigns to that specific interface. Combined, the two halves are designed to make every network interface's MAC address globally unique, no two interfaces manufactured for genuine use are supposed to share the same MAC address, ever, anywhere in the world.

An important property of the MAC address is that it is flat rather than hierarchical: it carries no information about where in the network the interface is located, unlike an IP address, whose structure often does reflect network location. This makes MAC addresses well suited for a very specific, local job: identifying devices on the same physical network segment, such as the same WiFi network or the same wired Ethernet segment, so that switches on that segment can deliver data to exactly the right interface without needing to know anything about the wider internet. A MAC address is not generally useful for finding a device across the broader internet, that is precisely the job the next section's concept, the IP address, was designed to solve.

Consider a worked example inside a single home network. Your laptop's WiFi interface has a MAC address, and your smart TV's WiFi interface has a different one, even though both devices are connected to the very same home WiFi network. When your home router's WiFi radio sends out data meant specifically for your laptop, it addresses that data to your laptop's MAC address, and your laptop's interface recognizes the data as its own and accepts it, while your smart TV's interface, seeing a MAC address that is not its own, ignores it. This local, direct delivery based purely on the hardware identity of the interface is exactly what MAC addresses exist to make possible.

Because a MAC address stays attached to a specific interface and says nothing about network location, it behaves very differently from the address covered next. Where the MAC address answers which exact interface, on this local network segment, is this, the IP address exists to answer a much bigger question: where, across the entire interconnected network, can this interface be found.
